markup: By {1963,|nineteen sixty-three,} a man had borrowed over {$150 million...|a hundred and fifty million dollars...}
against tanks that were mostly water.
Meet Tino {De Angelis,|Dee An-jeh-lis,} New Jersey's salad oil king.
His giant tanks were full of cooking oil.
Banks lent him money against it.
American Express sent inspectors to check.
But Tino's own men would climb up, drop a tape inside, and shout down:
{"90%|Ninety percent} full!"
And the inspector, on the ground... believed them.
So the banks lent more.
And more.
Soon, his papers showed more of that oil than the entire United States had.
But what if someone did look inside?
Then, in November {1963,|nineteen sixty-three,} his big bet on oil prices crashed.
His company went bust.
Lenders finally checked the tanks.
Inside...
was mostly water.
You see, oil floats on water.
Ever left salad dressing out?
The oil always rises to the top.
Fill a tank with water, add a thin layer of oil,
and from the hatch, it looks full.
And the real oil?
He pumped it through pipes, tank to tank,
so the same oil got counted again and again.
The hardest-working oil in America.
When it came out, American Express shares crashed.
But one young investor bought those shares cheap.
He bet people still trusted the brand.
His name?
Warren Buffett.
The oil was fake.
The trust was real.
